newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani cellular phone company resumes service.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani cellular phone company resumes service.

text.p: One of Pakistan's three cellular telephone companies has restored services in Karachi after dropping a compensation claim for losses arising from an 18-month suspension, a company executive said on Sunday.
"The service was restored yesterday at 2200 (1700 GMT)," said Sikander Naqi, general manager of operations at Instaphone, the brand name used by Pakcom Ltd, a subsidiary of Luxembourg's Millicom.

The previous government led by ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto cut off mobile telephone, payphone and pager services in Karachi and Hyderabad in July 1995 as part of its drive against militants of the ethnic Mohajir National Movement (MQM).

It was not immediately known when the other two cellular telephone operators, Paktel Ltd, a Cable & Wireless subsidiary, and Pakistan Mobile Telecommunications, known locally as Mobilink, which is a joint venture of U.S.-based Motorola Inc and local Saif Telecom.
Brian Holbutt, chief executive of Paktel Ltd, said he could not say when his company would be able to restore services because it had no government permission to do so.
"We have not been given the permission yet but we are still discussing the issues with Ministry of Communication," he said.
"The problem is this linkage between compensation and restoration which Paktel and Mobilink have a problem with."
The three companies had been coordinating their efforts to persuade Meraj Khalid's caretaker government to restore the services without waiving their compensation claims.

But Instaphone's decision to break ranks appeared to leave its rivals little choice but to follow suit and accept what they regard as an unsatisfactory offer made by the government to meet industry grievances over tax and other terms, analysts said.

Naqi said Instaphone previously had 12,000 clients in Karachi, Pakistan's biggest city and commercial hub. "We do not know what happened in the last 18 months, but we are quite hopeful the clients will be with us," he told Reuters.
Instaphone said it had accepted the conditions linked to the government's interim relief package, which promises negotiations on reducing custom duties, taxes and central excise duty.
"Instaphone has agreed not to seek compensation if the interim relief package is immediately implemented and operations in Karachi and Hyderabad are resumed immediately," it said.
"However, the interim relief package will be renegotiated at the end of 1997 for further relaxation for the cellular industry operators," it added, without elaboration.
During the ban, the mobile phone operators, a pager company and three payphone firms stayed ready to resume business in Karachi, representing about 40 percent of the Pakistan market.

The three phone companies have invested at least $160 million since 1990, but say they have an average negative return on capital employed of 36 percent. They suffered combined losses of 2.2 billion rupees ($54.7 million) during the ban.
